title: Nepal court gives green light to 'controlled' cannabis cultivation - Times of Suriname
description: Nepal court gives green light to 'controlled' cannabis cultivation  Times of Suriname
publisher.title: Times of Suriname
full_article: a petitioner in the case told AFP on Thursday. The Supreme Court ordered the government to make the "necessary arrangements" for the "controlled cultivation and production of cannabis". The framework would allow cultivation for medicinal, scientific, agricultural, horticultural and industrial purposes. The court also asked for wider consultations on recreational use. The ruling was issued in May 2025, but court documents were destroyed in a fire that September during protests that toppled the government. Its full text was released only this week. "We feel grateful to the Supreme Court for this verdict”, Saroj Adhikari, one of the petitioners, told AFP . Nepal revoked licences for cannabis dealers in 1973 under international pressure during a US-led campaign against drugs. Before that, Kathmandu had been a magnet for cannabis enthusiasts, with thousands of foreign backpackers flocking to buy hashish from government-licensed shops. Former health minister Birodh Khatiwada has long called for the ban to be lifted. "The decision came after a long wait”, said Khatiwada, who sponsored a related parliamentary motion in 2020. "Many developed nations have adopted legal cultivation, and we should not delay for it”, he added, arguing that regulation could create jobs and generate income while curbing illegal trade. "It will also help to curb illegal smuggling of marijuana, from which only a few people are benefiting”, Khatiwada told AFP . Cannabis has deep historical roots in Nepal, where it grows wild and its stems, leaves and resin have traditionally been used in food, textiles and traditional remedies. Each year, hundreds of holy men gather at Kathmandu's Pashupatinath temple, honouring the Hindu god Shiva, where they smoke openly. Elsewhere, however, penalties remain harsh. Marijuana dealers face up to 10 years in prison, and police seize and destroy thousands of cannabis plants each year. "The law restricts smoking marijuana”, Adhikari said. "But it's very common, so instead of restricting it, if it is regulated by law with strong enforcement mechanisms, it can generate revenue for the nation." ( Bssnews )

title: Duty amid disaster: Nepal floods weigh heavily on Gurkhas as they pass out at Catterick - Forces News
description: Duty amid disaster: Nepal floods weigh heavily on Gurkhas as they pass out at Catterick  Forces News
publisher.title: Forces News
full_article:
Gurkhas pass out after tough training in UK – and tragedy at home

Three hundred and twenty Nepali recruits have completed Phase 1 and 2 infantry training – officially becoming professional Gurkhas. The soldiers who passed out at ITC Catterick earned their places in the British Army from an initial pool of more than 13,000 applicants. But their achievement comes against a backdrop of personal tragedy.

The Doko race: Endurance, strength and resilience – but in Pirbright, not Nepal

No sleep but fighting on: Gurkha recruits on their toughest training exercise yet

Fish and chips at the seaside: Gurkha recruits go on curious but crucial training exercise

In August, catastrophic floods and landslides struck Nepal, directly impacting the families and villages of some of the recruits. It gave the parade added significance and made the achievements of the young Gurkhas all the more remarkable. Nine long months This year's intake of recruits to the Brigade of Gurkhas arrived from Nepal in February. BFBS Forces News was there as the men landed at Manchester Airport before crossing the Pennines to the Infantry Training Centre, Catterick – their home for the next nine months. Unlike non-Gurkha recruit training, Nepali soldiers undergo additional courses to learn English and understand British cultural life. That included trips to places like London and Whitby, where some of the recruits experienced the seaside for the first time. BFBS Forces News also joined the recruits at various stages of their infantry training. This included an early-stage fieldcraft exercise, an advanced urban warfare exercise and one of their final tests in the field – the infamous Defence Ex, which sees recruits digging trenches for days on end. Another key moment came when the recruits learned which unit within the Brigade of Gurkhas they had been selected for, with many securing positions in one of the two Royal Gurkha Rifles battalions.

The Gurkhas give an eyes right as they march past Lieutenant General Zac Stenning, who led the passing out parade at ITC Catterick (Picture: BFBS)

Nepal floods Since then, the men have been focused on reaching the end of training and joining their new units. But it was during this final stretch that Nepal was hit by the worst floods and landslides in generations – a disaster that brought widespread devastation, weighing heavily on the young men training in North Yorkshire. Yet the Gurkhas are nothing if not a brotherhood. During this difficult period, the recruits pushed through training, closely supported by their corporals and permanent staff. While remaining focused on the task at hand, the recruits and training staff raised thousands of pounds for domestic disaster relief efforts. A proud day Some of the new Gurkhas spoke moments after the passing out parade concluded. One of the soldiers, Private Roshan Thapa, who is joining the Gurkha Staff and Personnel Support (GSPS) branch of the Adjutant General's Corps, said the day had been one of the most significant of his life. "I'm feeling very happy and proud," he said. "This day will be the most memorable day of my life." They were sentiments echoed by others, including Private Kabin Phagami, who is also joining the GSPS. "I feel absolutely amazing. I'm really proud to be a part of the Gurkhas," he told me. "The training was really hard and tough, but at the end of all the sacrifices I made, I'm standing here and I'm proud of what I did."

Top general leads parade The passing out parade was led by one of the Army's top generals, Lieutenant General Zac Stenning, Commander Land Forces. He told the soldiers they had joined the Gurkhas at a pivotal time, and that their service would be vital in an increasingly volatile world. The 320 new Gurkhas will now take well-earned leave over the coming weeks before joining their battalions or embarking on trade-specific training across the UK. Selection for next year's intake of Gurkhas is already underway in Nepal.

full_article:
Photo by Solen Feyissa on Unsplash

Kathmandu, November 6

Nepal has formally launched the Visit Nepal campaign in collaboration with the Nepal Tourism Board and social media platform TikTok, aiming to promote the country to the global tourism market through digital content and storytelling.

The campaign, which began on Friday, seeks to showcase Nepal’s natural beauty, unique culture, heritage and diverse tourism experiences to audiences worldwide by highlighting historical significance and using digital technology and creative content.

The launch event was organised by the Tourism Board and TikTok in collaboration with the Nepal government, with Minister for Information and Communications Dr Bikram Timilsina attending as the chief guest.

Running until the end of 2026, the campaign is expected to promote Nepal as a tourism destination while connecting local creators, entrepreneurs, businesses and communities with the digital economy.

Speaking at the event, Minister Timilsina said digital platforms had transformed how people around the world discover tourist destinations. He said such platforms should be used to promote Nepal’s tourism, art, culture and entrepreneurship.

“Digital platforms have changed the way the world discovers destinations. A story shared from one corner of the world can inspire someone in another corner to visit Nepal,” he said. “We welcome TikTok as a potential long-term partner in connecting Nepal’s tourism, culture, creativity and young people with the world.”

Sunil Sharma, acting director of the Tourism Board’s Public Relations and Promotion Department, described the partnership as an important initiative that would add a new dimension to Nepal’s destination promotion strategy.

As part of the campaign, nine international travel content creators from Europe, the Middle East, Southeast Asia and South Asia are visiting various tourist destinations in Nepal and sharing their experiences with global audiences. They are scheduled to remain in Nepal from October 30 to November 7.

A dedicated Visit Nepal hashtag page has also been launched on TikTok to strengthen the campaign. The Tourism Board will collaborate with Nepali celebrities and local content creators through TikTok’s Collab feature to promote Nepal’s distinct identity and local perspectives. Livestreams will also be conducted from different tourist destinations.

Emir Gelen, TikTok’s head of government relations and public policy for the Middle East, Eurasia and Africa, said the partnership would help showcase Nepal’s tourism potential to the world while enabling local creators and small businesses to benefit from the digital economy.

Earlier, TikTok and the Nepal Tourism Board had jointly provided digital storytelling training to more than 300 local tourism entrepreneurs and content creators.

title: Momo, mon amour: A Nepali bill of fare — and affair - The Kathmandu Post
description: Momo, mon amour: A Nepali bill of fare — and affair  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Chatpate , vegetable momo, chicken momo, pork momo, chowmein, and the like. Nothing unusual about the ubiquitous items on the bill of fare in any restaurant in and around Kathmandu.

But wait. There’s something unusual. It’s not Kathmandu, but Geneva — at Bunsnpice - Momo & More, a cosy eatery located near Lake Geneva, the Jet d'Eau and Plage des Eaux-Vives.

On the door is a little message, accompanied by a rainbow flag, which reads: “Everyone is Welcome Here.” And to welcome everyone, Shakti Karki and Abhishek Pathak are there.

Photo: Bunsnpice - Momo & More/Instagram

Karki, 37, from Biratnagar, and Pathak, 31, from Birtamod, are a couple who have been running the establishment for the last four months in the Swiss city.

But behind the familiar menu is a story of love, courage and starting afresh in a foreign land.

Karki went to Switzerland to study in 2008. After finishing his studies, he joined a company as an intern, received a job offer and started working there. He returned to Nepal during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, when he met Pathak on Tinder, a dating app.

Karki returned to Geneva after four months, but he remained in touch with Pathak.

“The long-distance relationship was difficult,” Karki said. “We wanted to be together, so we decided to get married.”

But it was easier said than done. When they asked around, their friends told them there could be considerable complications despite Nepal’s legal recognition of same-sex marriage. Another problem was that Pathak did not have a visa.

Karki thought he would rather return to Nepal. And he did come to Nepal in October 2024. He wanted to be with his family — and his partner, who came to pick him up at the airport.

But no sooner had Karki landed in Nepal than Pathak’s visa arrived. The plan changed.

“We were booking the return tickets for both of us as soon as I landed back,” Karki chuckled.

The couple eventually registered their marriage in Geneva.

Karki had always loved cooking, but he wanted to turn his hobby into something productive. He found a partner who equally loved experimenting in the kitchen.

“We started the restaurant, then he took over and expanded it,” said Karki of his partner.

It all started with momo.

“We usually used to make momo on weekends and sell them throughout the week,” said Pathak. “Shakti helped me in the evening after he returned from his office. I am the cook, the server and the delivery man.”

Karki said the restaurant was Pathak’s idea.

“Because, like him, I too love food, cooking and trying new dishes. Then I found the financer,” said Pathak, flirtatiously looking at Karki.

Photo: Bunsnpice - Momo & More/ Instagram

What began as making momo at home and delivering them around the city gradually grew into a restaurant.

For Pathak, opening a restaurant was not just about cooking. When he arrived in Geneva, he first focused on learning French. He also started working in an Indian restaurant as a trainee, where he gained practical experience and learned the skills needed to run an establishment of his own.

As the conversation moved beyond food and their restaurant, they were happy to share how their relationship blossomed. After their first date in Bhedetar, Dharan, they gradually became part of each other’s lives, visiting one another’s homes.

Pathak would introduce Karki to his family as a friend. His mother liked Karki, although she did not know about their relationship.

“When I told my mother about our plans to marry and move to Geneva, I was not quite sure about the response,” he said. “But to my surprise, she said ‘okay’.”

Pathak at his restaurant in Geneva. Krishana Prasain/TKP

Pathak said his mother told him that she knew about LGBTQ+ people and that, as a parent, she did not want to complicate her children’s lives.

She later informed Pathak’s father about the relationship, and the family eventually accepted their decision.

For Karki, coming out to his family was a more difficult process.

He had kept his feelings to himself for a long time. But the pressure of hiding his identity, coupled with expectations of getting married, eventually became suffocating.

“So one day I told my mom about myself,” he said. “She cried at first after hearing about me but was supportive later.”

Karki’s mother later shared the news with other family members and relatives. When the couple returned to Nepal to attend a relative’s wedding, they were surprised by the support they received.

“This time I actually felt happy being myself,” Karki said.

Despite Nepal’s legal recognition of same-sex marriage, the couple said they encountered awkward and embarrassing moments during the marriage registration process in Nepal.

“If you want to get married, the form has only Mr. and Ms. options,” said Pathak.

The experience made them realise that legal recognition alone was not enough. Administrative procedures and the attitudes of officials also needed to change. They felt that officials were still taken aback when they encountered same-sex couples seeking to register their marriages.

Having built a life together in Geneva, Pathak is now keen to explore more of Europe and does not see himself returning to Nepal for at least another decade.

Photo: Bunsnpice - Momo & More/ Instagram

“I want to expand,” he said. “I want to open more restaurants in Geneva, maybe in the future. I want to adopt children from Nepal, if possible. We want to raise them here and then maybe, in retirement, I can go back to Nepal.”

Karki plans to be part of those dreams.

“Abhishek still needs to experience life here and travel a bit, as he has just started life here,” he said. “I’ll join him for the restaurant in a few months, and then we’ll see where life goes.”

But establishing a restaurant in Geneva has not been easy.

The couple said opening an eatery involves several procedures, from completing hygiene courses and finding a suitable location to obtaining permission for even small details, including putting up a signboard outside.

“We are still in the process of getting permission for so many things,” Pathak said. “We had permission for takeaway in the beginning, and later we wanted to have a sitting restaurant. For that, you need to hire someone who has completed a more advanced hygiene course.”

The requirements and costs also vary depending on the type of establishment. Running a dine-in restaurant involves higher taxes and additional responsibilities. Businesses must submit detailed plans covering the layout of the premises, seating capacity, security arrangements and emergency evacuation procedures.

Abhishek Pathak(left) and Shakti Karki at Bunsnspice-Momo & More, Geneva. Krishana Prasain/TKP

The couple now have a small kitchen and a dining area. They have also hired a local person to help them run the establishment.

Despite the challenges, they are determined to establish BunsNSpice as a place where people can discover, taste and enjoy Nepali food.

Interestingly, they said, customers from other backgrounds are often more enthusiastic about trying their food than Nepalis living in Geneva, who are already familiar with the flavours.

“For us, our focus clients are not Nepalis,” Pathak said. “Demand-wise, we can’t really say there is a demand for Nepali food because people don’t know the food. But when people try our food and come back, we are trying to create an environment here.”

The couple opened BunsNSpice using their savings. The restaurant also offers takeaway through Uber Eats.

Momo, chowmein and thukpa are among its most popular items. They are now planning to expand the menu with Nepali tapas , including bhutan and sekuwa .

Listening to the couple’s story, it becomes clear that BunsNSpice - Momo and More is about much more than food. It is about two people who found each other, chose to build a life together and turned their shared passion into a livelihood in a city far from home.

title: Floods in Nepal raise questions on the impact of climate change in the Himalayas - The Guilfordian
description: Floods in Nepal raise questions on the impact of climate change in the Himalayas  The Guilfordian
publisher.title: The Guilfordian
full_article:
A flash flood swept through Nepal in late August. Now, scientists warn that melting glaciers may endanger tens of millions of people living around the Himalayan region.

On Aug. 26, a chunk of a glacier, possibly 2,000 feet wide, according to The New York Times, between Nepal and China broke off and slid down the Himalayan mountains, accumulating debris and ice that fell into the Trishuli River, damming it and causing catastrophic flooding downstream.

The flood swept through Nepal, smashing through Nepali buildings and infrastructure. Twenty-four miles of road and 19 bridges were destroyed, as well as schools and hydropower plants, Nepali officials said.

In the immediate aftermath of the flood, more than 900 people were reported missing and at least 389 have died in Nepal.

Rajendra Pudasaini, an Essex nurse, spoke to the Press Association about the damage and death brought by the flood.

“They’re gone. The speed the water came, they couldn’t be saved, they were just swept away,” Pudasaini said.

Nepal’s tourism board said 391 tourists, including 291 foreigners, were reported missing in Nepal after the floods. Of the tourists were 100 visitors from India, a dozen Britons, and at least three Americans. Some citizens of Australia, the Netherlands, Malaysia, and South Africa were also reported missing.

The glacial collapse occurred on the Nepal side of the Himalayas, Nepalese officials said. Countries around the world have begun sending aid to Nepal. The UK is planning to send $6.6 million in aid, while the US State Department is already providing $500,000.

“This is one of the most devastating floods I can remember seeing in this region,” said Tenzing Chogyal Sherpa, an expert in atmospheric and water processes at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, on Aug. 26.

Even after the initial incident, the search for the missing continued, and Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority reported a new total of 5,200 people remain missing, including 636 foreigners, and 1,399 dead.

According to Laura Bicker in Beijing, the danger in Nepal and the surrounding area remains high, as a lake of rising water that could soon overflow has formed along the China-Nepal border.

David Fisher, head of a delegation for the Red Cross in Nepal, told the BBC News that secondary flood warnings have put people “very on edge.”

In 2021, a similar glacier break caused major flooding in the northern Indian state of Uttarakhand, killing more than 100 people. Experts believe disasters like these might only become more frequent in the future. In a 2023 report by Miriam Jackson, a Norwegian cryosphere researcher, Jackson found that glaciers melted 65 percent faster from 2010 to 2019 than in the decade before.

“We are going to see more of these events,” Jackson said.

The Hindu Kush Himalayan range is home to 40,000 glaciers . Of these glaciers, only 21 are being tracked. The article by World Weather Attribution “ Rapid Warming in the Himalaya Exacerbates Geohazard Cascades Beyond Adaptation Limits” concludes that “ the resulting debris flood was therefore likely caused by several sources of water, including melting glacier ice, water stored beneath the glacier and in permafrost, ice and water carried within the debris”

A New York Times reporter, Somni Segupta, reported that further melting could threaten the communities native to the Himalayan range with more floods.

Jackson and other experts urge leaders across the region to prepare for similar disasters in the future by increasing monitoring in the area and exchanging data.

“We need a lot more data-sharing and communications across these national borders,” Jackson told the Times.

title: Foreign Minister Khanal to lead Nepali delegation to COP31 in Turkiye - The Rising Nepal
description: Foreign Minister Khanal to lead Nepali delegation to COP31 in Turkiye  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov 5: Minister for Foreign Affairs, Shisir Khanal, is leaving for Antalya, Turkiye on November 7, leading a Nepali delegation to the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).

The UN climate event is scheduled from November 9 to 20. Minister Khanal will address the Opening Plenary of the COP31 on November 9, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The Minister will also participate in the Leader’s Summit on November 11-12.

Foreign Minister Khanal also participates in various high-level events including ‘Advancing the Mountain Agenda: Glaciers, Cryosphere and Resilience under Overshoot, Shared Responsibility and Sustainable Financing’, jointly hosted by Nepal, Tajikistan, Kyrgyz Republic, Bhutan and Pakistan.

There are also sideline events for him to attend and hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts and other dignitaries.

The Nepali delegation comprises Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment, Gita Chaudhary; Member of the National Planning Commission, Prof Dr Sanjaya Acharya; Secretary of the Agriculture, Forest and Environment Ministry, Dr Rajendra Prasad Mishra; and other senior government officials.

Minister Khanal is scheduled to return home on November 14, the Ministry added. (RSS)

title: From Yak cheese to political barbs: PM Balen’s Facebook posts keep Nepal talking - myRepublica
description: From Yak cheese to political barbs: PM Balen’s Facebook posts keep Nepal talking  myRepublica
publisher.title: myRepublica
full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nov 6: Balen Shah, who frequently made headlines by sharing his views on social media while serving as mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City, has continued the same practice since becoming prime minister. His Facebook posts have increasingly become a platform for debate on government decisions, administrative activities, political controversies and matters of public concern.

(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});

His communication style has also sparked debate, with questions being raised over his preference for using his personal social media accounts rather than formal press conferences or official government statements to communicate with the public. While some posts have provided updates on government decisions, others have triggered fresh speculation and controversy in political circles.

It has almost become routine for one of the prime minister’s posts to attract hundreds of thousands of reactions and subsequently become a news story. The attention surrounding Balen’s posts, however, goes beyond their popularity. They have also raised questions about the government’s communication strategy, public accountability and the nature of political discourse.

A Prime Minister Who Knows How to Make a Post Go Viral

One of Balen’s most widely discussed posts since becoming prime minister promoted yak cheese. On May 16, 2026, he shared a photograph of yak cheese produced by the state-owned Dairy Development Corporation (DDC) on Facebook, accompanied by the message, “Say cheese, DDC’s cheese.”

His post received praise for promoting a product made by a government-owned corporation. By the time this report was prepared, it had attracted around 495,000 likes and more than 48,000 comments. Reports also emerged after the post that public interest in and sales of DDC products had increased.

Earlier, on May 9, he had shared a photograph of himself wearing a white shirt, striped trousers, white shoes and black sunglasses. After he also posted a TikTok video in the same outfit, social media users began recreating his look and using artificial intelligence (AI) to generate similar photographs. Even the prime minister’s clothing became a social media trend.

These two posts demonstrated that Balen’s use of social media extends beyond political communication. He has also used Facebook to promote government products, shape his personal image and establish direct connections with the public.

Using Facebook to Defend Government Decisions

Among Balen’s posts after becoming prime minister, his statements on managing landless people and informal settlers also drew considerable attention.

Related story Rasuwa produces cheese worth Rs 59 m

On May 4, 2026, he said the government would relocate citizens living in unsafe locations to safer and better-managed areas. He added that decisions concerning other landless citizens would be made based on recommendations from the relevant commission and the data it had collected.

The message conveyed through his post was that the government did not intend to displace citizens but was seeking a permanent solution to the problem while ensuring their right to housing. In this way, the prime minister used his personal Facebook page to defend government decisions and reassure the public.

Similarly, he used social media to justify the government’s decision to dissolve student and employee organisations and to express his views on other policy matters.

A Two-Word Message That Set Off Debate

Balen’s brief social media post also attracted attention after the government unveiled its budget. When the budget for fiscal year 2026/27 was presented, he posted a short message on Facebook at 9:54 pm, saying, “Rest assured.”

The brief statement prompted various interpretations on social media. Some criticised the discussion for shifting away from the budget’s priorities, weaknesses in economic policy and government plans towards speculation about what the prime minister meant by his post.

A Dig at the Politics of Ambassadorial Appointments

Another widely discussed post by Balen after becoming prime minister concerned ambassadorial appointments.

On June 6, 2026, he wrote on Facebook: “I also want to become an ambassador. If anyone has the PM’s number, please share it with me.”

Balen made the sarcastic remark after reports emerged that government secretary Krishna Hari Pushkar had sent a message to the prime minister expressing his interest in becoming an ambassador. Ministers and leaders from the ruling party also responded to the post with humorous comments.

However, the post also triggered debate over whether it was appropriate for someone holding the office of prime minister to make sarcastic remarks about a sensitive administrative matter such as appointments. Some interpreted his comment as a jibe at political manoeuvring in appointments, while others criticised it in relation to the dignity of the prime ministerial office.

A Cryptic Warning That Invited Speculation

On November 1, Prime Minister Balen published another cryptic post. He wrote: “When the time is right, everyone will have their bad days. No one should dream that one or two people will escape.”

Although he did not name any individual or incident, the statement came amid criticism of the government over an alleged case involving a middleman’s contact with a judge and the deployment of police personnel at media outlets.

The prime minister’s political adviser, Kumar Ben, also responded to the post with a comment along the lines of, “When will the right time come?” This further fuelled discussion in political and media circles about the intended meaning of the prime minister’s message.

A Political Message That Raised Eyebrows

Balen’s latest widely discussed post appears to concern the political priorities of the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) and other political parties.

On the night of Kartik 19, he wrote on Facebook: “Your cadres fight while your leaders sit back and laugh; our leaders fight, and humanity holds on to hope! That is the only difference! There is a difference between saving the country and saving a party.”

The post appeared a few hours after RSP Chairperson Rabi Lamichhane, speaking at a programme in Chitwan, said the party had not instructed the government to remove the inspector general of police and that the government itself should justify its decision.

The prime minister did not disclose whom he was referring to in the post. However, its timing and wording have prompted various interpretations and speculation in political circles.

When a Personal Facebook Page Becomes a Government Mouthpiece

As Balen’s posts continue to attract attention, another important question has emerged: To what extent should a prime minister’s personal Facebook page serve as a channel for official government communication?

The discussion has also highlighted the difference in follower numbers between the two platforms. Balen’s personal Facebook page has more than 4.6 million followers, while the Facebook page of the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers has considerably fewer.

Santosh Sigdel, executive director of Digital Rights Nepal, has said that the use of personal social media accounts to disseminate information may reflect a desire to reach a large audience quickly, while also potentially involving the financial earnings generated through social media platforms. The prime minister’s press and research adviser, meanwhile, has said the government has a policy of using both official and personal platforms in an organised manner.

The prime minister’s personal popularity and the credibility of official government information are not the same thing. Therefore, government decisions, policies and official information concerning citizens also need to be regularly communicated through institutional government channels.

Balen’s posts have demonstrated their ability to immediately capture public attention, initiate political debate and become subjects of media coverage. However, the likes, comments and shares they receive cannot be considered a complete representation of public opinion. Popularity on social media and actual public sentiment can differ.

There was a time in Nepali politics when people had to attend rallies and public gatherings to hear what political leaders had to say. Today, however, public interest increasingly centres not just on what leaders say but also on what they write on Facebook. Prime Minister Balen’s posts have made this shift even more apparent.

One post explains a government decision, another draws attention to a domestic product in the market, while yet another sparks political debate between those in power and the opposition. This shows how social media in Nepali politics has evolved beyond a platform for leaders to express their views. It has become a powerful tool for shaping political agendas and influencing public discourse.

publisher.title: India Tribune - Chicago
full_article:
Sehwag, Raichandani fifties help India thrash Nepal by ten wickets in U-19 Asia Cup opener/ Credit: BCCI Domestic/x

Muscat, Nov 6 (IANS) Aaryavir Sehwag and skipper Lakshya Raichandani struck unbeaten half-centuries as India thrashed Nepal by 10 wickets in their first Men's Under-19 Asia Cup match at the Al Amerat Cricket Ground here on Friday.

Chasing a modest 129, Aaryavir and Raichandani finished off the runs in only 19.1 overs. Earlier, fast bowler Ishan Sood’s three-wicket burst with the new ball ensured Nepal were bowled out for 128 in 42.3 overs.

After electing to bowl first on a pitch that carried a thin layer of grass, Sood moved the ball both ways and beat the bat repeatedly in an opening spell of six overs. That effort led to Sood picking three wickets as the Nepal batters struggled to get going. Sood finished with figures of 3-18 from his 10 overs bowled on the trot, including four maidens.

Darsh Sonar (43 off 93 balls) steadied the innings after the early collapse by adding partnerships of 24 and 43 respectively with Niraj Yadav and Aashish Luhar to push Nepal past 100. Once Sonar’s partnership with Luhar was broken, Nepal’s lower order fell apart. Left-arm spinner Arjun Rajput took three wickets and Yashveer Goud had two scalps as Nepal were all out for 128.

By the time India’s chase began, the new ball did not swing much. Aaryavir and Raichandani played out the first few overs carefully before they began hitting boundaries at regular intervals. Aaryavir, son of former India opener Virender Sehwag, went after the Nepal spinners.

He often stepped out of the crease to loft the ball down the ground and reached his half-century off just 34 balls. Raichandani was content in rotating the strike while Aaryavir took the attacking route, and later brought up his own fifty off 59 balls.

The comprehensive victory completed with 185 balls remaining ensured India took to the top of Group A with two points and a net run rate of 4.170. India will next face arch-rivals Pakistan in their second Group A clash on Sunday.

Brief Scores: Nepal 128 in 42.3 overs (Darsh Sonar 43, Aashish Luhar 29; Arjun Rajput 3-8, Ishan Sood 3-18) lost to India 129/0 in 19.1 overs (Aaryavir Sehwag 70 not out, Lakshya Raichandani 53 not out) by ten wickets

title: Nepal seeks stronger recognition of mountain issues in UN climate process - Climate Home News
description: Nepal seeks stronger recognition of mountain issues in UN climate process  Climate Home News
publisher.title: Climate Home News
full_article:
In the wake of its recent glacial flooding disaster, Nepal and the kingdom of Bhutan have proposed a new agenda item on mountains and climate change for the COP31 summit which opens on Monday in the Turkish city of Antalya.

In a submission addressed to the COP31 presidency and the head of the UN climate secretariat (UNFCCC), Nepal said the agenda item, entitled “1.5°C Warming in Mountains”, is an effort to strengthen the response of the international community to the climate risks facing the world’s mountain regions.

The item proposes that mountain issues should become a regular part of the formal UN climate change process, with a focus on scientific assessment of the risks associated with warming overshooting 1.5C, an annual high-level dialogue, a dedicated work programme and improved access to climate finance.

Maheshwar Dhakal, chief of the climate change management division of Nepal’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment, told Climate Home News that Himalayan countries face similar problems such as collapsing glaciers and flooding from glacial lakes.

“We are trying to bring all Himalayan countries together under this agenda item,” he said.

COP31 Briefing: What to expect from the Antalya climate summit?

At this year’s UN General Assembly, Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah called for strong global action to ensure climate justice and proposed creating a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by India, China and Nepal. It would share satellite data, monitor glacial slopes and lakes, strengthen early warning systems and coordinate cross-border disaster response.

Nepal has experienced significant infrastructure losses and human casualties from flooding every year since 2020. In late August, the collapse of a glacial slope on the border with Tibet caused a torrent of water and debris to course down the Bhote Koshi River, leaving more than 6,000 people dead or missing.

According to a government needs assessment, the disaster caused an estimated $2.7 billion in physical damage and economic losses, while around $4.8 billion will be required for recovery and reconstruction.

More research needed on threats

Although high mountain regions are known to be fragile ecosystems, especially as global warming accelerates glacier melt, the extent of their vulnerability is still not fully understood. When the devastating Bhote Koshi floods hit, it opened the eyes of the world to the risks.

Dhakal said the Bhote Koshi floods “have proved the impacts of climate change in the Himalayan region”, which were linked to rising temperatures by scientists with the World Weather Attribution group. “Therefore, Nepal wants scientific studies, research and political discussions on mountain climate risks to receive greater attention at international climate conferences,” he added.

Nepal has been making efforts on this front since 2009, when it held a cabinet meeting at Kalapatthar near Mount Everest. Since COP28 in Dubai, Nepal has organised high-level events and dialogues on mountain issues at COPs and is co-hosting one at COP31 with Bhutan, Pakistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

Editor’s Desk: Nepal’s disaster has laid bare the world’s adaptation accountability gap

Dhakal said the dialogues held so far have raised awareness, but mountain concerns must become part of the formal UN climate process to unlock climate finance and technical support that can bolster countries’ capacity to tackle climate threats.

If specific indicators and priorities are developed for mountain regions, vulnerable developing countries like Nepal would have better access to finance to help them adapt to the climate warming they have done very little to cause, he added.

More detailed data would enable them to prepare stronger project proposals for international climate funds, including the Green Climate Fund (GCF). In 2025, the GCF backed a project to protect livelihoods from climate-induced flooding in Nepal but it took seven years to get approval.

Sindhu Dhungana, an alternate board member at the GCF, said the problem is becoming more widespread and urgent for the Hindu Kush Himalaya region.

“The economies, cultures and almost everything in Himalayan countries depend on mountains,” he explained. “For us, climate change is mountain change… [it has] affected everything, including the economy and biodiversity.”

Debris and mud cover buildings in DevGhat village in Nepal (Photo: Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images) Debris and mud cover buildings in DevGhat village in Nepal (Photo: Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images)

Destroyed development projects

Nepal wants the UN climate process to address mountain risks both before and after disasters. Countries need better research, technology, early warning systems and other adaptation measures to protect people and infrastructure. But even when countries take precautions, loss and damage is likely to occur and will require international support to address it.

Nepal has been provisionally allocated $21.6 million from the United Nations' new Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) to help with the aftermath of the Bhote Koshi disaster, but this is just a fraction of needs and the money will come only months after it made an initial request.

Dhakal pointed to the damage caused by floods to infrastructure built with loans, such as the Melamchi Drinking Water Project, which received $312 million from the Asian Development Bank but was destroyed by a major flood in 2021, shortly after it began operating. The recent Bhote Koshi disaster wiped out a dozen hydropower facilities, as well as solar energy systems.

Nepal flood destruction shows “limits to adaptation”, scientists say

Nepal wants international discussions on what should happen when climate-related disasters destroy development projects built using credit, and how the loans should be treated afterwards.

"Climatic disasters wash out… projects, but the burden of loan is still paid by Nepal," Dhakal said.

For now, it remains unclear whether the opening session of COP31 will consider or adopt the proposed agenda item on mountains and climate change, with consultations on how to respond still underway among governments and the COP31 co-presidencies.

"If countries agree to discuss the proposal and include it in the agenda, that would be another step forward," Dhakal said. "Further discussions in the coming years could gradually give the mountain agenda a stronger shape."

title: Nepal’s Loss and Damage Claim After the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster: A Timely Decision, Yet Structural Gaps Remain - South Asian Voices
description: Nepal’s Loss and Damage Claim After the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster: A Timely Decision, Yet Structural Gaps Remain  South Asian Voices
publisher.title: South Asian Voices
full_article:
On August 26, 2026, a massive rock-ice avalanche in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi border region, large enough to register a seismic signal equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, triggered an extreme debris torrent that cascaded more than 150 kilometers down the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridor. The disaster decimated critical infrastructure along the river, indefinitely closed a vital trade corridor highway, wiped out over 10 percent of Nepal’s generation capacity, and left about 1,451 dead and more than 5,000 missing as of September 21, according to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). A World Weather Attribution analysis found that human-caused warming of about 1.5°C in July and August near the site, together with permafrost degradation and glacier thinning, may have weakened a slope already geologically primed to fail.

Five days after the avalanche, Nepal’s Finance and Environment Ministers formally invoked the Governing Instrument of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD). An operating entity of the financial mechanism of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) established in 2023, the FRLD finances responses to loss and damage from climate impacts in developing countries, funded by donor pledges and run by a Board that decides on funding requests. In response to Nepal’s request, eight board members demanded an extraordinary meeting outside of its usual schedule. On October 22, the FRLD held its first-ever extraordinary meeting, which resulted in a provisional set-aside of USD $21.6 million, making Nepal the first country to receive such an earmark.

By climate finance standards, this turnaround represents an unprecedented velocity—one that was made possible by an ad hoc Board decision, not the system. Yet measured against Nepal’s assessed needs in this ongoing humanitarian emergency, it is a sobering reminder of the structural limitations of the Fund itself: a cap of USD $20 million per request, no standing rapid-response window, and thin capital.

Nepal will not be the last country to require such loss and damage funds after a disaster. In that light, the question of whether this recent chain of extraordinary procedural events can be reified in the FRLD’s permanent fund-disbursement architecture is all the more urgent. Three decisions before the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) in Türkiye and the next Board meeting can settle this debate in the short-to-medium term and help shore up the Fund’s ability to support countries undergoing severe environmental disasters in the years to come: quickly approving Nepal’s proposal, establishing a permanent rapid-response window, and offering real capital behind the pledges.

“Nepal will not be the last country to require such loss and damage funds after a disaster. In that light, the question of whether this recent chain of extraordinary procedural events can be reified in the FRLD’s permanent fund-disbursement architecture is all the more urgent.”

A Historic Decision, an Inadequate Response

The FRLD pays for losses already suffered, whereas climate funds mostly finance projects that cut emissions or build resilience in advance. Each follows its own approval path. Understanding the discrepancy between the funding mechanisms at the Fund’s disposal—both the established pathway and the ad hoc one that arose around the Nepal floods—is crucial for contextualizing the positions in which Nepal and the FRLD each now find themselves.

The Barbados Implementation Modalities (BIM) are the Fund’s interim start-up route, designed for testing and learning, with a cap of USD $20 million per request. Countries submit a full funding request during a call window, which the Fund’s Secretariat assesses against the standard BIM criteria—country-led approaches, expected results, and fit with national priorities—before the Board makes its decision. The Long-Term Model, which the Board will begin shaping at the 10th Board meeting (B10) in Manila in December, will set the Fund’s permanent access rules. That means that the Fund did not have a rapid-response procedure when the Nepal floods occurred in August and still does not have one now.

Nepal has made two requests under the BIM this year. The first request, filed during the call that closed on June 15, 2026, was for USD $20 million. The Kathmandu Post reported that it had been approved, but the Board deferred its first funding decisions under the BIM to B10 in December, and no funds have been released. Nepal’s August 31 letter following the floods, which asked for a special Board decision absent a rapid-response pathway, requested a further USD $20 million, the maximum request amount under the BIM. This was the request that the Board responded to on October 22, where Nepal was awarded a set-aside of USD $21.6 million, including USD $1.6 million for oversight fees. The set-aside is additional to the BIM envelope, so it does not draw on it.

It is important to acknowledge that this amount, which is also not yet paid out, covers less than 0.5 percent of the more than USD $4.7 billion that NDRRMA puts as its need for post-disaster repair and reconstruction. But while the headline numbers seemed to signal institutional agility, the October 22 meeting revealed operational fractures with implications for how the Fund handles future disasters. That the Nepal set-aside rested on an ad hoc process outside the BIM’s regular cycle has caused board members like Japan’s Kazuho Taguchi to stress that this “strictly exceptional” response does not prejudge the design of the Long-Term Model. Germany, for its part, said the Board must also protect the Fund’s integrity and fairness to all other applicants during the BIM phase and beyond, while still drawing lessons from Nepal’s response. On the other hand, Pakistan’s representative, Ali Tauqeer Sheikh, supported the decision but remarked that the text was “much narrower than we had discussed and proposed,” sets no timeframe for approval, and predetermines Nepal’s needs by existing BIM allocations. Pakistan speaks from experience: Its post-disaster needs assessment after massive floods in 2022 put recovery and reconstruction needs at no less than USD $16.3 billion.

But it is precisely this question of precedent and lessons learned—of whether rapid response becomes standing Fund policy or stays a one-off—that is perhaps the most consequential part of the October 22 outcome. The difference matters for any country that will suffer a climate disaster in the future: With a standing window in place, it could invoke a settled process to seek funding, whereas if rapid response remains a one-time exception, it will have to start from scratch to negotiate its own special decision, as Nepal did over 52 days from the August 31 letter to the October 22 decision.

Towards Permanent Architecture

Nepal is already bearing losses of the kind that a loss and damage fund is meant to address. Research on a 2021 debris flood in the Melamchi Valley found average household losses of USD $52,113 against just USD $380 in support received. Mountain disasters also strike national finances. After a glacial lake flood destroyed the main border bridge at Rasuwagadhi in July 2025, trade through the crossing fell about 95 percent within six months, as earlier Stimson Center analysis documented from government customs records—a kind of loss that existing climate finance is not designed to capture. The August 2026 flood hit the same corridor and also halted Nepal’s electricity exports to Bangladesh, which had been flowing under a three-country power-trade arrangement since late 2024. The interruption was partial and temporary: Seasonal exports of 40 megawatts (MW) to Bangladesh, routed through India’s grid under a 2024 agreement between the Nepal Electricity Authority and the Bangladesh Power Development Board, resumed in late October with different plants supplying power. Whether the Fund’s framework can recognize losses felt across borders remains an open question.

For now, Nepal’s experience presents the international community with a specific set of institutional decisions that cannot wait for COP31’s general commitments. Three things must change before COP31 in Türkiye and B10 in Manila can be considered progress, not just process. The Board holds the pen on the first two, COP31 guidance to the Fund can reinforce them, and the third rests with donors.

First, Nepal’s project proposal must be approved on an expedited basis. Pakistan requested and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) encouraged approval between scheduled meetings rather than at B10, while the Co-Chair said she would “strive to adapt,” but the Board must commit to a specific timeline at or before B10. That also requires the Fund to offer guidance to Nepal on what to submit in the first place.

Second, the Nepal pilot must be codified as a permanent rapid-response modality under the Long-Term Model, which the Board will begin to shape at B10 in December. If codified, the pilot would become a standing window that could shape future allocations to countries suffering after major disasters. A codified window would need three features: a defined trigger, a first tranche of up to USD $20 million (the BIM cap), and a decision in weeks rather than the 52 days the Nepal case needed. That there was a second extreme flow event in Nepal, the October 11 Budhi Gandaki flood in Gorkha, underscores the need to establish such a window sooner rather than later. The legal basis for this already exists: Tamim Alothimin of Saudi Arabia grounded developed-country obligations in Article 4.3 of the UN climate convention and Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, and civil-society observers added Articles 4.4 and 4.5 of the convention—provisions that, put plainly, place obligations on developed countries to provide finance and support. With their framing of obligations rather than voluntary pledges, these provisions would also give the Fund a firmer basis for predictable capital, one of the other decisions it must make. B10 should begin from that more robust legal footing.

“The case of Nepal showed that the Board can move fast. Now the Fund must show Nepal, and the world, that it can deliver at scale.”

Third, the Fund must have enough capital to operate at the scale its mandate requires. The Fund’s funding page lists USD $719.46 million in total contributions as of November 4, but only about USD $486 million had actually been received as of July 31, against calls for at least USD $400 billion a year by 2035 from a campaign backed by more than 250 organizations in April. The Fund’s current pipeline shows the strain: 176 funding requests from around the world, amounting to a combined USD $2.8 billion, are competing for the USD $342 million the Board has allocated to the BIM. This means that a single country like Nepal, with both its earlier BIM request and the August 31 request, could notionally draw about USD $40 million, about 8 percent of that USD $486 million. Only its earlier request, of up to USD $20 million, would come from the USD $342 million BIM envelope.

As examples of climate finance turnaround times, the Green Climate Fund (GCF) took seven years, from a 2018 concept note to approval in 2025, to clear a USD $49.9 million glacial lake outburst flood project outside the Bhotekoshi basin; a second Nepal project, the Alternative Energy Promotion Centre’s clean cooking project, received its first disbursement in January 2024, more than four years after its concept note. By contrast, the FRLD went from Nepal’s request to a decision in a remarkably agile 52 days—but to a set-aside, not an actual disbursement. Nepal’s proposal has yet to clear assessment, and approval at B10 in December, if it comes, would be under four months after the letter. COP31 should write a standing rapid-response window into the Fund’s permanent rules so that an emergency like Nepal’s no longer needs its own Board decision.

COP31, set to begin on November 9, is the first place to press these issues. Nepal’s position paper, presented at the National Climate Summit on October 29, should put them on record, and Nepal’s pavilion in Antalya will showcase the Bhotekoshi-Rasuwa floods. Nepal and Bhutan have also formally proposed a COP31 agenda item on 1.5°C warming in mountains, including mountain priorities in loss and damage arrangements. The marker to watch in this immediate period is whether donor statements or COP31 guidance to the Fund address the rapid-response window.

Following COP31, the FRLD’s own 11th Board meeting comes to Nepal on March 17–19, 2027, making Nepal both a claimant and host. That meeting will present an opportunity for Nepal and the Least Developed Countries (LDC) Group to ask donors in the room for three things: moving Nepal’s own proposal from set-aside to disbursement; creating a standing rapid-response window under the Long-Term Model; and turning promised pledges to the Fund into paid-in capital, or money that the Fund has actually received. The case of Nepal showed that the Board can move fast. Now the Fund must show Nepal, and the world, that it can deliver at scale.

title: Fund the flood warnings that Nepal never got - Bangkok Post
description: Fund the flood warnings that Nepal never got  Bangkok Post
publisher.title: Bangkok Post
full_article:
The upcoming UN climate summit in Turkey from Nov 9-20 will once again misuse a catastrophe to get attention. This year, the summit will highlight the tragedy in Nepal, where an ice-and-rock avalanche tore through the northern part of the country in late August. The disaster has left more than 1,400 dead and 5,000 missing and a recovery bill of nearly US$5 billion (167 billion baht), about an eighth of the country's economy. And yes, it carries a lesson for the world, just not the one campaigners are selling: ever bigger climate budgets.

Just days after the disaster, the UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, declared that climate change is making such tragedies "much more likely, frequent and severe". Climate activist Bill McKibben wrote that Nepalis "are not causing the crisis that is killing them: we are".

Climate change may well have played a part. The World Weather Attribution group, which rarely understates the case, finds that human-caused warming raised Himalayan summer temperatures by about 1.5C. Yet even it calls climate change "a destabilising factor acting on a pre-existing geological predisposition, rather than the fundamental cause". The largest study of snow avalanches across High Mountain Asia, published this year, mapped 60 million of them since 1990.

Either way, carbon cuts are not the answer. If every country at the summit pledged deeper cuts and, for once, kept its word, the glaciers of Langtang would not refreeze. Trillions of dollars spent cutting carbon buy a barely measurable drop in temperature by the end of the century.

What the Trishuli Valley needed is no mystery. A flood becomes a mass-casualty disaster when the people in its path are not warned in time. Some areas were too close to warn, but others had 40 minutes or more.

Downstream in Bidur, principal Rajendra Dawadi evacuated and saved some 900 students minutes before the flood swept his school away. His warning came by word of mouth, not by siren.

Nepal's own damage assessment calls for more monitoring, repairs to wrecked stations, and sirens and text alerts along the rivers. The initial cost is a trivial $2.3 million.

Nearly 30% of all development money for Nepal went to climate: more than $3 billion committed in 2020-24. Nearly half a billion dollars went to power lines and smart meters to swap fossil fuels for hydropower, in a country that already gets almost all its electricity from water. German aid committed €6 million (225.1 billion baht), three times the cost of a warning system, to solar panels to cut CO₂ emissions.

Even programmes that should have helped lost their way. A $150 million World Bank disaster-resilience program from 2024 promised better warnings, then spread itself across droughts, wildfires, heat waves, building-code compliance and other rivers.

The Green Climate Fund came closest. In 2020, it approved $27.4 million to make the Gandaki River basin, which includes the Trishuli, more resilient to floods and landslides. None of it went to sirens or flood alerts. Instead, a large part went to irrigation, which helps with drought, not floods, plus farmer schools, ecotourism and a gender action plan. A $50 million project for sensors, sirens and backup communications sat in the fund's pipeline for seven years before approval in 2025. It began work in March and is due to finish in 2033.

The World Meteorological Organization estimates that spending $800 million on early warning in poor countries would avoid $3 billion to $16 billion in losses a year. Bangladesh lost more than 300,000 people to a cyclone in 1970; since 2007, forecasts, shelters and drills have kept its annual cyclone deaths under 200.

Growth is the adaptation policy that covers every hazard at once. Extreme poverty fell from 55% of the population in 1995 to under 1% in 2022. But although average growth since 1996 has been 4.2% per year, most South Asian economies have grown faster. The fixes are unglamorous: more power generation, better roads to let exporters compete, fewer regulatory hurdles, and a better deal for the migrants whose remittances make up a quarter of the economy.

A richer Nepal builds sturdier bridges, sites its dams and roads more carefully, keeps its sensors running and pays for its own sirens.

There is something perverse about campaigners using yet another disaster to demand more of the policies that failed its victims. If the upcoming climate summit wants to honour the dead of the Trishuli Valley, it should pay for the warning systems they never got, then get out of the way of Nepal's growth.

Bjorn Lomborg is President of the Copenhagen Consensus, Visiting Fellow at Stanford University's Hoover Institution, and author of 'False Alarm' and 'Best Things First'.
